title: The first words, again
hook: salaam, bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah: once vocabulary, now a map; and a neighbor's peace
tomorrow: which story would you tell a kid who feels stuck?

segments.voice: Yesterday: home at last, with peace at every door and at the last gate. The journey home is done. The summit starts here, by looking back at where it all began.

The first words anyone learns in a new language are tiny: hello, thanks, see you. This path started small too: bismillah was its very first word, and inshallah came a few days later. Set them beside two more, salaam and alhamdulillah, and you have four little words. Back then they were vocabulary. Now, after the long road since, they look different: a map of a single day, and of a whole life.
screen: `HELLO, THANKS, SEE YOU.` → `FOUR LITTLE WORDS.` → `NOW, A MAP.`

segments.voice: Salaam, peace: how you meet anyone, at any door. Bismillah: how you begin. The Qur'an opens with it, in Pickthall's words: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." Alhamdulillah: how you respond, the very next line: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Inshallah: how you face tomorrow. The Qur'an tells the Prophet never to say of anything, I'll do that tomorrow, without adding: if Allah wills. Meet, begin, thank, hope. That's a day. Stretch it out, and it's a life. Now a neighbor. Jewish neighbors greet with peace too, shalom aleichem, peace be upon you. And the Torah's blessing for the people ends on it, in the JPS words: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." What's shared: both put peace into the most ordinary moment there is, hello. One honest difference: in the Torah, that blessing is given to Aaron and his sons, the priests, to say over the people. As-salamu alaykum is said by anyone to anyone, and the Qur'an asks the one greeted to answer with the same or better. And a line for anyone who greets you: in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says spreading salaam is how people come to love one another.

segments.voice: Say the four slowly, one on each breath: salaam, bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah. With each one, name the moment in your own day where it belongs: a door, a start, a thank-you, a plan. Go around again if there's time.
screen: `ONE WORD PER BREATH.` · `A DOOR, A START.` · `A THANK-YOU, A PLAN.`

segments.voice: The first words: salaam, bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah. Meet in peace, begin with Allah's name, thank Him, and leave tomorrow in His hands.
Keep this one for the summit: four words, a whole life, from the first door to the last. Day one of the summit, counted.

howItsDone: Muslims greet with as-salamu alaykum and answer wa alaykum as-salam, say bismillah before eating, starting work or travel, alhamdulillah after meals and good news, and inshallah when speaking of the future.

chat.says: back in Chicago for finals. Talia said 'shalom!' when i walked in. i said 'salaam!' we laughed. same word?
options: Close: both greet with peace, and shalom ends the Torah's priestly blessing. Shared, not identical.
Exactly the same. Every faith says the same thing about peace, just in another language.
Different. Shalom is just hello; salaam is a prayer meant only for other Muslims.
chat.meaning: Both traditions put peace into hello. The Torah's blessing ending in peace is given to the priests; salaam is said by anyone and answered.
